knownFor: The killing of Eric V of Denmark on the night of 22 November 1286
The outlawing of Marshal Stig Andersen Hvide and eight others in 1287
The chapel of penance later built on the site
The memorial cross raised in 1891 on the six hundred and fifth anniversary
overview: The village associated with the 1286 murder of Eric V of Denmark.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Finderup in central Jutland became infamous as the site of the murder of Eric V of Denmark on 22 November 1286. Eric was killed in his bed by noble conspirators, one of the most politically significant assassinations in medieval Danish history.

The village lies about ten kilometres south-west of Viborg, which is the reason the king was there at all: Viborg was the assembly place of Jutland, where kings were acclaimed and the provincial thing met, and Finderup was a night’s lodging on the road to it.

contentSections.title: The night of 22 November 1286
paragraphs: The king had been hunting and took shelter for the night in a barn at Finderup. Armed men came in during the night and killed him where he lay. The tradition that the body was found riddled with wounds belongs to the ballads and the later chronicles rather than to any surviving record of the corpse, and the number of wounds usually quoted cannot be traced to a contemporary source.

What is not in doubt is the fact and the date. Eric V was buried in Viborg Cathedral, a few hours’ ride from where he died, and Denmark had a nine-year-old king in Eric VI and a regency under his mother.

contentSections.title: Who killed the king
paragraphs: At the assembly held at Nyborg at Whitsun 1287 nine men were condemned in absentia for the killing, among them Marshal Stig Andersen Hvide and Count Jacob of Halland. They were outlawed and their lands forfeited; they fled to Norway, were given shelter there, and spent the following years raiding the Danish coast from the island fortress of Hjelm.

The verdict was political rather than forensic. The reign had been a long quarrel between a crown trying to tax and judge and a nobility that had forced the charter of 1282 on the king, and the men condemned were the leaders of that opposition. Danish historians have argued ever since over whether the court convicted the guilty or the inconvenient, and the surviving evidence does not settle it.

contentSections.title: The chapel, the cross and the barn
paragraphs: A chapel of penance was built at the site during the fourteenth century, of the kind raised where a great crime needed expiation, and it stood until the crown gave permission to demolish it in the middle of the sixteenth century.

The barn itself has never been located. A modern reading of the evidence holds that the original parish church of Finderup stood where the memorial cross now is — excavation there found the remains of a church-like building about 25 by 9 metres — and that the present parish church is the old chapel of penance. If that is right, the altar of today’s church stands where the king was killed; it is an argument from buildings, not a proof.

contentSections.title: The site today
paragraphs: A memorial cross stands on the western edge of the village, paid for by the poet Thor Lange and unveiled on 22 November 1891, six hundred and five years to the day after the killing.

Eric’s murder at Finderup remained officially unsolved, though Marshal Stig Andersen was widely blamed and forced into exile. The killing reflected deep conflict between the Danish crown and the aristocracy over royal authority and noble privilege. The fallout shaped Danish constitutional conflict for a generation.

name: Finderup
summary: The Jutland village where Eric V of Denmark was killed in a barn on the night of 22 November 1286 — a crime never solved in law, marked since 1891 by a cross on the supposed spot.

timeline.title: The charter
timeline.description: Eric V is forced to grant a charter binding the king to hold a yearly assembly and to rule by law.

timeline.title: The killing
timeline.description: The king is killed in a barn at Finderup during the night while lodging on the road to Viborg.

timeline.title: Burial at Viborg
timeline.description: Eric V is buried in Viborg Cathedral; his nine-year-old son succeeds as Eric VI.

timeline.title: The outlawry
timeline.description: Nine men, including Marshal Stig Andersen Hvide, are condemned in absentia at the assembly at Nyborg.

timeline.title: Raids from Hjelm
timeline.description: The outlawed men, sheltered in Norway, raid the Danish coast from the island fortress of Hjelm.

timeline.title: A chapel of penance
timeline.description: A chapel is built at the site of the killing as expiation.

timeline.title: The chapel demolished
timeline.description: The crown grants permission to pull the chapel down.

timeline.title: The memorial cross
timeline.description: A cross funded by the poet Thor Lange is unveiled on the six hundred and fifth anniversary.
